q: A team wants a repeatable way to describe how they take a Claude-powered feature from initial concept through iterative development, release, and ongoing operation. A vendor pitches a proprietary 'AI Development Lifecycle' framework built specifically for LLM-based projects, arguing that generic IT frameworks predate large language models and can't account for non-deterministic behavior.
o: Adopt the vendor's proprietary AI Development Lifecycle, since generic IT frameworks predate LLM applications
Rely on prompt engineering best practices alone, since they govern how the feature behaves in production
Apply the generic systems life cycle (plan, develop, test, implement, operate, maintain) using Agile or DevOps practices, adding evals as the test gate
Design a new lifecycle framework from scratch, since no existing framework accounts for non-deterministic model output
e: The objective is scoped as generic IT systems life cycle management; Claude-application work maps onto the same plan-develop-test-implement-operate-maintain arc as any other system, with Agile or DevOps supplying the iteration and release discipline and evals replacing exact-match tests as the quality gate. Adopting a proprietary 'AI-specific' framework is the trap this objective is built to catch — an engineered-to-sound-plausible distractor that ignores that the generic model already covers this arc. Prompt engineering is a technique applied during development, not a lifecycle framework in its own right. Building a new framework from scratch overstates the problem: non-determinism is handled by changing what the existing test gate checks, not by discarding the gate.

q: A Claude-powered pipeline is already live in production. An engineer wants to bump the pinned model version and adjust two prompts. Company policy requires a documented change record, a risk assessment, and sign-off from a change advisory board before any modification reaches production, regardless of how small the change is. Which management discipline governs this requirement?
o: Scrum sprint planning, since the change can be scoped and sized as a backlog item
Waterfall requirements sign-off, since the system's original scope must be honored
DevOps continuous deployment, which is designed to automate this kind of approval away
e: Documented change records, risk assessment, and change advisory board sign-off before any production modification, no matter how small, is the definition of ITIL-style service management governing a live system. Sprint planning organizes how development work gets scheduled and estimated, not how a change to a live production system gets approved. Waterfall governs how a project's own phases are sequenced during initial build, not ongoing change control after go-live. DevOps automates delivery pipelines, but 'automates approval away' directly contradicts the stem's explicit requirement for a human sign-off — a distractor that sounds efficient while ignoring the stated constraint.
